+# ADR 0001: Increase Pricing Cache TTL from 900s to 3600s
+
+## Status
+
+Accepted
+
+## Context
+
+The pricing service currently caches pricing data with a Time-To-Live (TTL) of 900 seconds (15 minutes). This was established as a conservative default to balance between reducing database load and ensuring pricing data remained relatively fresh. However, analysis of pricing update patterns shows that pricing changes are infrequent—typically occurring no more than a few times per day during business hours—and existing price staleness of 15 minutes has not resulted in user-facing issues or reported discrepancies.
+
+The current 900-second TTL creates unnecessary cache evictions and cache misses, generating redundant queries to the pricing database. With typical request volumes, this results in approximately 15-20% of pricing requests requiring database lookups rather than serving from cache. The cost of these redundant queries is measurable in both database load and latency for end-users who experience uncached lookups.
+
+## Decision
+
+We will increase the pricing cache TTL to 3600 seconds (1 hour). This change is low-risk given the operational characteristics of pricing updates and will significantly reduce database load while remaining acceptable for business requirements. The 1-hour window aligns with typical pricing update windows and provides a 4x improvement in cache efficiency without introducing unacceptable staleness.
+
+We chose 3600 seconds over other candidates (e.g., 1800s / 30 minutes) because the benefits of reduced load scale with TTL length, and the marginal risk of 1 hour versus 30 minutes is minimal given that pricing updates are not real-time-sensitive operations. Teams responsible for pricing changes will continue to use cache invalidation mechanisms when out-of-band updates occur.
+
+## Consequences
+
+**Positive:** Cache hit rates will increase from approximately 80% to 95%+, reducing database queries by an estimated 50% for pricing reads. This directly decreases database load and improves response latency for cached requests. The reduction in database contention may also improve performance for other non-cached queries during peak traffic.
+
+**Negative:** There is a small increase in the maximum age of stale pricing data from 15 minutes to 1 hour. In the unlikely scenario where a pricing update is made without triggering cache invalidation, affected users could see outdated pricing for up to 60 minutes. This is an acceptable trade-off given the low frequency of pricing changes and the existence of cache invalidation procedures.
+
+**Mitigation:** Cache invalidation endpoints should be tested and monitored to ensure they function as expected. Monitoring should track cache hit rates post-deployment to validate the expected improvement.
